claim: The planetary biosphere is powered by a suite of key metabolic innovations that emerged early in the history of life.
source: The planetary biosphere is powered by a suite of key metabolic innovations that emerged early in the history of life.
evidence: This is a general statement about the biosphere drawing from established scientific understanding.

claim: Microbes access atmospheric sources of bioessential nitrogen through the activities of just one family of enzymes, nitrogenases.
source: Today, microbes access atmospheric sources of bioessential nitrogen through the activities of just one family of enzymes, nitrogenases.
evidence: This statement reflects established scientific knowledge about nitrogen fixation.

claim: The only dinitrogen reduction mechanism known to date is an ancient feature conserved from nitrogenase ancestors.
source: Here, we show that the only dinitrogen reduction mechanism known to date is an ancient feature conserved from nitrogenase ancestors.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data on ancestral nitrogenases.

claim: Ancestral nitrogenase genes were phylogenetically reconstructed and inserted into the genome of Azotobacter vinelandii.
source: We designed a paleomolecular engineering approach wherein ancestral nitrogenase genes were phylogenetically reconstructed and inserted into the genome of the diazotrophic bacterial model, Azotobacter vinelandii, enabling an integrated assessment of both in vivo functionality and purified nitrogenase biochemistry.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: Nitrogenase ancestors are active and robust to variable incorporation of one or more ancestral protein subunits.
source: Nitrogenase ancestors are active and robust to variable incorporation of one or more ancestral protein subunits.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from engineered strains.

claim: All ancestors exhibit the reversible enzymatic mechanism for dinitrogen reduction, specifically evidenced by hydrogen inhibition.
source: Further, we find that all ancestors exhibit the reversible enzymatic mechanism for dinitrogen reduction, specifically evidenced by hydrogen inhibition, which is also exhibited by extant A. vinelandii nitrogenase isozymes.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data on hydrogen inhibition.

claim: Life may have been constrained in its sampling of protein sequence space to catalyze one of the most energetically challenging biochemical reactions in nature.
source: Our results suggest that life may have been constrained in its sampling of protein sequence space to catalyze one of the most energetically challenging biochemical reactions in nature.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results involving speculation about evolutionary constraints.

claim: The evolutionary history of life on Earth has generated tremendous ecosystem diversity, the sum of which is orders of magnitude larger than that which exists at present.
source: The evolutionary history of life on Earth has generated tremendous ecosystem diversity, the sum of which is orders of magnitude larger than that which exists at present (Jablonski, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Jablonski, 2004.

claim: The early histories of many of life's key metabolic pathways and the enzymes that catalyze them remain coarsely resolved.
source: However, the early histories of many of life's key metabolic pathways and the enzymes that catalyze them remain coarsely resolved.
evidence: This reflects current scientific understanding about gaps in knowledge.

claim: Phylogenetic inference has been used to advance understanding of early metabolic innovations.
source: Important efforts to advance understanding of early metabolic innovations have included phylogenetic inference (Gold et al., 2017; Sánchez-Baracaldo and Cardona, 2020)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gold et al., 2017 and Sánchez-Baracaldo and Cardona, 2020.

claim: Systems-level network reconstructions have been used to advance understanding of early metabolic innovations.
source: Important efforts to advance understanding of early metabolic innovations have included phylogenetic inference (Gold et al., 2017; Sánchez-Baracaldo and Cardona, 2020), systems-level network reconstructions (Goldford et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Goldford et al., 2017.

claim: Extant or mutant biological models have been leveraged as proxies for ancient counterparts to advance understanding of early metabolic innovations.
source: Important efforts to advance understanding of early metabolic innovations have included phylogenetic inference (Gold et al., 2017; Sánchez-Baracaldo and Cardona, 2020), systems-level network reconstructions (Goldford et al., 2017), and the leveraging of extant or mutant biological models as proxies for their ancient counterparts (Zerkle et al., 2006; Soboh et al., 2010; Hurley et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zerkle et al., 2006; Soboh et al., 2010; Hurley et al., 2021.

claim: Methods to directly study metabolic evolutionary histories across past environmental and cellular transitions remain underexplored.
source: However, methods to directly study these metabolic evolutionary histories across past environmental and cellular transitions remain underexplored.
evidence: This reflects the current state of the field based on scientific knowledge.

claim: Phylogenetic reconstructions of enzymes can be directly integrated within laboratory microbial model systems.
source: To address this, phylogenetic reconstructions of enzymes can be directly integrated within laboratory microbial model systems (Garcia and Kaçar, 2019; Kacar et al., 2017b; Kędzior et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Garcia and Kaçar, 2019; Kacar et al., 2017b; Kędzior et al., 2022.

claim: Predicted ancestral enzymes can be 'resurrected' within a compatible host organism for functional characterization in a paleomolecular framework.
source: In this paleomolecular framework, predicted ancestral enzymes can be 'resurrected' within a compatible host organism for functional characterization.
evidence: This describes the paleomolecular approach based on established methodology.

claim: Both phylogenetic and geological evidence indicate that the origin of biological nitrogen fixation was a singular and ancient evolutionary event.
source: Both phylogenetic and geological evidence (Garcia et al., 2020; Raymond et al., 2004; Boyd et al., 2011a; Stüeken et al., 2015; Parsons et al., 2021) indicate that the origin of biological nitrogen fixation was a singular and ancient evolutionary event on which the modern biosphere has since been built.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to Garcia et al., 2020; Raymond et al., 2004; Boyd et al., 2011a; Stüeken et al., 2015; Parsons et al., 2021.

claim: The only known nitrogen fixation pathway is catalyzed by an early-evolved family of metalloenzymes called nitrogenases.
source: The only known nitrogen fixation pathway (compared to, for example, at least seven carbon-fixation pathways [Garcia et al., 2021a]) is catalyzed by an early-evolved family of metalloenzymes called nitrogenases that reduce highly inert, atmospheric dinitrogen (N2) to bioavailable ammonia (NH3).
evidence: This reflects established scientific knowledge with a citation to Garcia et al., 2021a for comparison.

claim: There are at least seven carbon-fixation pathways.
source: The only known nitrogen fixation pathway (compared to, for example, at least seven carbon-fixation pathways [Garcia et al., 2021a])
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Garcia et al., 2021a.

claim: Nitrogenases reduce highly inert, atmospheric dinitrogen (N2) to bioavailable ammonia (NH3).
source: The only known nitrogen fixation pathway (compared to, for example, at least seven carbon-fixation pathways [Garcia et al., 2021a]) is catalyzed by an early-evolved family of metalloenzymes called nitrogenases that reduce highly inert, atmospheric dinitrogen (N2) to bioavailable ammonia (NH3).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about nitrogenase function.

claim: The nitrogenase family comprises three isozymes that vary in their metal dependence (i.e. molybdenum, vanadium, and iron).
source: The nitrogenase family comprises three isozymes that vary in their metal dependence (i.e. molybdenum, vanadium, and iron) and, in certain cases, all coexist within the same host organism (Mus et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mus et al., 2018.

claim: In certain cases, all three nitrogenase isozymes coexist within the same host organism.
source: The nitrogenase family comprises three isozymes that vary in their metal dependence (i.e. molybdenum, vanadium, and iron) and, in certain cases, all coexist within the same host organism (Mus et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mus et al., 2018.

claim: Many diazotrophs depend on genetic strategies for coordinating the biosynthesis and expression of multiple nitrogenase isozymes and their respective metalloclusters.
source: Many diazotrophs depend on genetic strategies for coordinating the biosynthesis and expression of multiple nitrogenase isozymes and their respective metalloclusters (Pérez-González et al., 2021; Burén et al., 2020)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pérez-González et al., 2021; Burén et al., 2020.

claim: In oxic environments, diazotrophs protect oxygen-sensitive nitrogenase metalloclusters from degradation.
source: Many diazotrophs depend on genetic strategies for coordinating the biosynthesis and expression of multiple nitrogenase isozymes and their respective metalloclusters (Pérez-González et al., 2021; Burén et al., 2020), and, in oxic environments, protecting the oxygen-sensitive metalloclusters from degradation (Gallon, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gallon, 1992.

claim: Nitrogenase enzymes are a central component of a broader, co-evolving nitrogen fixation machinery.
source: Thus, nitrogenase enzymes are a central component of a broader, co-evolving nitrogen fixation machinery.
evidence: This is an inference based on the preceding discussion of nitrogenase complexity.

claim: Features of nitrogenase create significant experimental challenges for nitrogen fixation engineering.
source: These features that create significant experimental challenges for nitrogen fixation engineering (Smanski et al., 2014; Bennett et al., 2023; Burén and Rubio, 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Smanski et al., 2014; Bennett et al., 2023; Burén and Rubio, 2018.

claim: Nitrogenase features make this metabolism an ideal candidate for systems-level, paleomolecular study.
source: These features that create significant experimental challenges for nitrogen fixation engineering (Smanski et al., 2014; Bennett et al., 2023; Burén and Rubio, 2018) nevertheless also make this metabolism an ideal candidate for systems-level, paleomolecular study.
evidence: This is an inference about the suitability of nitrogenase for the study approach.

claim: How biological nitrogen fixation emerged and evolved under past environmental conditions is still poorly constrained relative to its importance in Earth's planetary and biological history.
source: How biological nitrogen fixation emerged and evolved under past environmental conditions is still poorly constrained relative to its importance in Earth's planetary and biological history.
evidence: This reflects the current state of scientific knowledge.

claim: Nitrogen has been a limiting nutrient over geological timescales.
source: Because nitrogen has been a limiting nutrient over geological timescales (Falkowski, 1997; Allen et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Falkowski, 1997; Allen et al., 2019.

claim: Nitrogenase has long been a key constituent of the expanding Earth's biosphere.
source: Because nitrogen has been a limiting nutrient over geological timescales (Falkowski, 1997; Allen et al., 2019), nitrogenase has long been a key constituent of the expanding Earth's biosphere.
evidence: This is an inference based on nitrogen limitation and the role of nitrogenase.

claim: The Haber-Bosch process is an energetically and environmentally costly workaround for nitrogen fertilizer production.
source: The impact of nitrogen limitation is underscored by human reliance on the industrial Haber-Bosch process, an energetically and environmentally costly workaround for nitrogen fertilizer production (Vicente and Dean, 2017)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Vicente and Dean, 2017.

claim: The Haber-Bosch process was designed to supplement a remarkable molecular innovation that biology has tinkered with for more than three billion years.
source: The impact of nitrogen limitation is underscored by human reliance on the industrial Haber-Bosch process, an energetically and environmentally costly workaround for nitrogen fertilizer production (Vicente and Dean, 2017) designed to supplement a remarkable molecular innovation that biology has tinkered with for more than three billion years.
evidence: This is an inference about the relationship between the Haber-Bosch process and biological nitrogen fixation.

claim: How the structural domains and regulatory network of nitrogenase were recruited remains an open question.
source: How the structural domains and regulatory network of nitrogenase were recruited (Boyd et al., 2015; Mus et al., 2019) and under what selective pressures the metal dependence of nitrogenases was shaped (Garcia et al., 2020; Boyd et al., 2011b) remain open questions.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Boyd et al., 2015; Mus et al., 2019.

claim: Under what selective pressures the metal dependence of nitrogenases was shaped remains an open question.
source: How the structural domains and regulatory network of nitrogenase were recruited (Boyd et al., 2015; Mus et al., 2019) and under what selective pressures the metal dependence of nitrogenases was shaped (Garcia et al., 2020; Boyd et al., 2011b) remain open questions.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Garcia et al., 2020; Boyd et al., 2011b.

claim: It is not known how the enzymatic mechanism for dinitrogen reduction has been tuned by both peptide and metallocluster to achieve one of the most difficult reactions in nature.
source: Importantly, it is not known how the enzymatic mechanism for dinitrogen reduction has been tuned by both peptide and metallocluster to achieve one of the most difficult reactions in nature (Seefeldt et al., 2020; Stripp et al., 2022; Harris et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Seefeldt et al., 2020; Stripp et al., 2022; Harris et al., 2019.

claim: Previous insights into nitrogenase sequence-function relationships have primarily derived from single or dual substitution studies.
source: At the enzyme level, previous insights into nitrogenase sequence-function relationships have primarily derived from single or dual substitution studies.
evidence: This reflects the current state of the field based on scientific knowledge.

claim: Single or dual substitution studies have often yielded diminished or abolished nitrogenase activity.
source: At the enzyme level, previous insights into nitrogenase sequence-function relationships have primarily derived from single or dual substitution studies. These have often yielded diminished or abolished nitrogenase activity (Seefeldt et al., 2020; Stripp et al., 2022)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Seefeldt et al., 2020; Stripp et al., 2022.

claim: In certain cases, single or dual substitution studies have improved nitrogenase reactivity toward alternate, industrially relevant substrates.
source: These have often yielded diminished or abolished nitrogenase activity (Seefeldt et al., 2020; Stripp et al., 2022), though in certain cases improved reactivity toward alternate, industrially relevant substrates (Seefeldt et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Seefeldt et al., 2020.

claim: The combination of detailed functional studies within an explicit evolutionary scheme has not previously been accomplished for the nitrogen fixation system.
source: Despite illuminating key features of extant nitrogenase mechanisms in select model organisms, the combination of detailed functional studies within an explicit evolutionary scheme has not previously been accomplished for the nitrogen fixation system.
evidence: This reflects the novelty of the current study based on knowledge of the field.

claim: An evolutionary systems biology approach was established for the cellular- and molecular-level characterization of ancestral nitrogenases resurrected within A. vinelandii.
source: Here, we seek guidance from the Earth's evolutionary past to reconstruct the history of the key metabolic enzyme, nitrogenase. We establish an evolutionary systems biology approach for the cellular- and molecular-level characterization of ancestral nitrogenases resurrected within the model diazotrophic bacterium, A. vinelandii.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: Variably replacing different protein subunits of the nitrogenase complex with inferred ancestral counterparts enables nitrogen fixation in A. vinelandii.
source: We find that variably replacing different protein subunits of the nitrogenase complex with inferred ancestral counterparts enables nitrogen fixation in A. vinelandii.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: Purified ancestral enzymes exhibit the specific N2 reduction mechanism retained by their studied, extant counterparts.
source: Purified ancestral enzymes exhibit the specific N2 reduction mechanism retained by their studied, extant counterparts, and maintain the same catalytic selectivity between N2 and protons.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data on purified enzymes.

claim: Purified ancestral enzymes maintain the same catalytic selectivity between N2 and protons as their studied, extant counterparts.
source: Purified ancestral enzymes exhibit the specific N2 reduction mechanism retained by their studied, extant counterparts, and maintain the same catalytic selectivity between N2 and protons.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data on purified enzymes.

claim: The core strategy for biological nitrogen fixation is conserved across the investigated timeline.
source: Thus, the core strategy for biological nitrogen fixation is conserved across the investigated timeline.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: A. vinelandii (strain 'DJ') is an ideal experimental model due to its genetic tractability and the availability of detailed studies on the genetics and biochemistry of its nitrogen fixation machinery.
source: We selected the obligately aerobic gammaproteobacterium, A. vinelandii (strain 'DJ'), an ideal experimental model due to its genetic tractability and the availability of detailed studies on the genetics and biochemistry of its nitrogen fixation machinery (Noar and Bruno-Bárcena, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Noar and Bruno-Bárcena, 2018.

claim: The extant A. vinelandii molybdenum-dependent nitrogenase is the best-studied isozyme relative to the A. vinelandii vanadium and iron dependent nitrogenases.
source: We specifically targeted the extant A. vinelandii molybdenum-dependent ('Mo-;) nitrogenase (hereafter referred to as wild-type, 'WT'), which is the best-studied isozyme (Seefeldt et al., 2020) relative to the A. vinelandii vanadium ('V-') and iron ('Fe-') dependent nitrogenases.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Seefeldt et al., 2020.

claim: The WT Mo-nitrogenase complex comprises multiple subunits, NifH, NifD, and NifK (encoded by nifHDK genes), which are arranged into two catalytic components: a NifH homodimer and a NifDK heterotetramer.
source: The WT Mo-nitrogenase complex comprises multiple subunits, NifH, NifD, and NifK (encoded by nifHDK genes), which are arranged into two catalytic components: a NifH homodimer and a NifDK heterotetramer (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is established knowledge about nitrogenase structure, also shown in Figure 1B.

claim: During catalysis, NifH and NifDK components transiently associate to transfer one electron from NifH to NifDK and subsequently dissociate.
source: During catalysis, both components transiently associate to transfer one electron from NifH to NifDK and subsequently dissociate.
evidence: This is established knowledge about nitrogenase catalytic mechanism.

claim: Transferred electrons accumulate at the active-site Mo-containing metallocluster ('FeMoco') housed within the NifD subunits for reduction of the N2 substrate to NH3.
source: Transferred electrons accumulate at the active-site Mo-containing metallocluster ('FeMoco') housed within the NifD subunits for reduction of the N2 substrate to NH3.
evidence: This is established knowledge about nitrogenase catalytic mechanism.

claim: A maximum-likelihood nitrogenase phylogeny was built from a concatenated alignment of NifHDK amino acid sequences.
source: To infer Mo-nitrogenase ancestors, we built a maximum-likelihood nitrogenase phylogeny from a concatenated alignment of NifHDK amino acid sequences (Figure 2A; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the phylogenetic methodology used in the study, with reference to figures.

claim: The phylogeny contains 385 sets of homologs representative of known nitrogenase molecular sequence diversity (including Mo-, V-, and Fe-nitrogenases).
source: The phylogeny contains 385 sets of homologs representative of known nitrogenase molecular sequence diversity (including Mo-, V-, and Fe-nitrogenases), and is rooted by dark-operative protochlorophyllide oxidoreductase proteins classified within the nitrogenase superfamily (Ghebreamlak and Mansoorabadi, 2020).
evidence: This describes the phylogenetic dataset used in the study.

claim: The phylogeny is rooted by dark-operative protochlorophyllide oxidoreductase proteins classified within the nitrogenase superfamily.
source: The phylogeny contains 385 sets of homologs representative of known nitrogenase molecular sequence diversity (including Mo-, V-, and Fe-nitrogenases), and is rooted by dark-operative protochlorophyllide oxidoreductase proteins classified within the nitrogenase superfamily (Ghebreamlak and Mansoorabadi, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ghebreamlak and Mansoorabadi, 2020.

claim: Anc1 has ~90% amino acid sequence identity to WT across the full length of concatenated NifHDK proteins.
source: For this study, we selected ancestors that fall within the direct evolutionary lineage of A. vinelandii WT (Figure 2B), 'Anc1' and 'Anc2' (listed in order of increasing age), having ~90% and~85% amino acid sequence identity to WT across the full length of their concatenated NifHDK proteins, respectively (Figure 2C; Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is data from the phylogenetic reconstruction shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Anc2 has ~85% amino acid sequence identity to WT across the full length of concatenated NifHDK proteins.
source: For this study, we selected ancestors that fall within the direct evolutionary lineage of A. vinelandii WT (Figure 2B), 'Anc1' and 'Anc2' (listed in order of increasing age), having ~90% and~85% amino acid sequence identity to WT across the full length of their concatenated NifHDK proteins, respectively (Figure 2C; Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is data from the phylogenetic reconstruction shown in Figure 2C.

claim: A relatively conservative percentage identity threshold was chosen based on prior studies benchmarking the functional expression of ancestral elongation factor proteins in Escherichia coli and Synechococcus elongatus.
source: A relatively conservative percentage identity threshold was chosen based on prior studies benchmarking the functional expression of ancestral elongation factor proteins in Escherichia coli (Kacar et al., 2017a) and Synechococcus elongatus (Kędzior et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kacar et al., 2017a and Kędzior et al., 2022.

claim: WT, Anc1, and Anc2 lie within a Mo-nitrogenase clade (previously termed 'Group I') that contains homologs from diverse aerobic and facultatively anaerobic taxa, including proteobacteria and cyanobacteria.
source: WT, Anc1, and Anc2 lie within a Mo-nitrogenase clade (previously termed 'Group I' [Raymond et al., 2004]) that contains homologs from diverse aerobic and facultatively anaerobic taxa, including proteobacteria and cyanobacteria (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Raymond et al., 2004 and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A maximum age constraint of ~2.5 Ga for Group I nitrogenases (and thus for both Anc1 and Anc2) can be reasoned based on the timing of the Great Oxidation Event and downstream emergence of aerobic taxa represented nearly exclusively within this clade.
source: A maximum age constraint of ~2.5 Ga for Group I nitrogenases (and thus for both Anc1 and Anc2) can be reasoned based on the timing of the Great Oxidation Event (Lyons et al., 2014) and downstream emergence of aerobic taxa represented nearly exclusively within this clade.
evidence: This is an inference based on geological knowledge and phylogenetic data, supported by a citation to Lyons et al., 2014.

claim: Residue-level differences between ancestral and WT nitrogenases ('ancestral substitutions') are broadly distributed along the length of each ancestral sequence.
source: Residue-level differences between ancestral and WT nitrogenases ('ancestral substitutions') are broadly distributed along the length of each ancestral sequence (Figure 1B; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: An ancestral substitution proximal to the active-site FeMoco metallocluster lies within a loop considered important for FeMoco insertion (NifD I355V).
source: An ancestral substitution proximal to the active-site FeMoco metallocluster lies within a loop considered important for FeMoco insertion (Dos Santos et al., 2004) (NifD I355V; residue numbering from WT) and is observed across all targeted NifD ancestors (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dos Santos et al., 2004 and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The NifD I355V ancestral substitution is observed across all targeted NifD ancestors.
source: An ancestral substitution proximal to the active-site FeMoco metallocluster lies within a loop considered important for FeMoco insertion (Dos Santos et al., 2004) (NifD I355V; residue numbering from WT) and is observed across all targeted NifD ancestors (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is data from the ancestral reconstruction shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Other ancestral substitutions are notable for their location at relatively conserved residue sites and/or within subunit interfaces, including two at the NifD:NifK interface that are proximal to one another, F429Y (NifD) and R108K (NifK).
source: Other ancestral substitutions are notable for their location at relatively conserved residue sites (assessed by ConSurf Ashkenazy et al., 2016; Figure 2—figure supplement 3; see Materials and methods) and/or within subunit interfaces, including two at the NifD:NifK interface that are proximal to one another, F429Y (NifD) and R108K (NifK).
evidence: This is data from the ancestral reconstruction, with conservation assessed by ConSurf (Ashkenazy et al., 2016) and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The Anc2 NifD protein contains five more ancestral substitutions at conserved sites than the younger Anc1 NifD protein.
source: The Anc2 NifD protein contains five more ancestral substitutions at conserved sites than the younger Anc1 NifD protein.
evidence: This is data from the ancestral reconstruction.

claim: In all studied ancestors, the C275 and H442 FeMoco ligands, as well as other strictly conserved nitrogenase residues, are retained.
source: In all studied ancestors, the C275 and H442 FeMoco ligands, as well as other strictly conserved nitrogenase residues, are retained.
evidence: This is data from the ancestral reconstruction.

claim: Extant nitrogenases within the Group I nitrogenase clade are associated with numerous accessory genes likely recruited to optimize the synthesis and regulation of the oxygen-sensitive nitrogenase for aerobic or facultative metabolisms.
source: Extant nitrogenases within the Group I nitrogenase clade (which include Anc1 and Anc2 descendants) are associated with numerous accessory genes likely recruited to optimize the synthesis and regulation of the oxygen-sensitive nitrogenase for aerobic or facultative metabolisms (Boyd et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Boyd et al., 2015.

claim: A. vinelandii WT is assembled and regulated with the help of >15 additional nif genes in addition to the structural nifHDK genes.
source: For example, in addition to the structural nifHDK genes, A. vinelandii WT is assembled and regulated with the help of >15 additional nif genes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about A. vinelandii nitrogenase.

claim: The extant descendants of Anc1 and Anc2 are primarily aerobic or facultative proteobacteria and are thus associated with higher complexity nif gene clusters.
source: Likewise, the extant descendants of Anc1 and Anc2 are primarily aerobic or facultative proteobacteria and are thus associated with higher complexity nif gene clusters (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The likely oxygen-tolerant, ancient proteobacterium harboring ancestral nitrogenases were similar in nif cluster complexity to extant A. vinelandii.
source: We hypothesized that the likely oxygen-tolerant, ancient proteobacterium harboring these ancestral nitrogenases were similar in nif cluster complexity to extant A. vinelandii.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on phylogenetic inference.

claim: The nif accessory genes present in A. vinelandii would support the functional expression of resurrected nitrogenase ancestors.
source: Thus, we predicted that the nif accessory genes present in A. vinelandii would support the functional expression of resurrected nitrogenase ancestors.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the hypothesis about nif cluster complexity.

claim: A. vinelandii strains harboring only the ancestral nifD gene from both targeted ancestral nodes ('Anc1A' and 'Anc2') express 'hybrid ancestral-WT' nitrogenase complexes.
source: First, we constructed A. vinelandii strains harboring only the ancestral nifD gene from both targeted ancestral nodes ('Anc1A' and 'Anc2'), thereby expressing 'hybrid ancestral-WT' nitrogenase complexes (Figure 1C).
evidence: This describes the experimental design shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The hybrid ancestral-WT nitrogenase strategy is similar to in vitro 'cross-reaction' studies that have evaluated the compatibility of nitrogenase protein components from differing host taxa.
source: This strategy is similar to in vitro 'cross-reaction' studies that have evaluated the compatibility of nitrogenase protein components from differing host taxa (Smith et al., 1976).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Smith et al., 1976.

claim: A strain harboring all Anc1 nifHDK genes expresses a fully ancestral nitrogenase complex ('Anc1B').
source: Second, we constructed a strain harboring all Anc1 nifHDK genes, expressing a fully ancestral nitrogenase complex ('Anc1B'; sequence reconstructed from a node equivalent to Anc1A from an alternate phylogeny, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: A. vinelandii strains were constructed by markerless genomic integration of ancestral nitrogenase genes.
source: A. vinelandii strains were constructed by markerless genomic integration of ancestral nitrogenase genes, as described in Materials and methods.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.

claim: All A. vinelandii constructs harboring ancestral genes enabled diazotrophic growth in molybdenum-containing, nitrogen-free media.
source: All A. vinelandii constructs harboring ancestral genes enabled diazotrophic growth in molybdenum-containing, nitrogen-free media.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: All strains had comparable doubling times to WT during the exponential phase (p>0.05).
source: All strains had comparable doubling times to WT during the exponential phase (p>0.05; Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Strain Anc2 had a ~14 hr increase in the lag phase relative to WT (p ≈ 2e-7).
source: The only significant difference among strains was a~14 hr increase in the lag phase of strain Anc2 relative to WT, harboring the oldest nitrogenase ancestor (p ≈ 2e-7).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: Growth was not detected under the same conditions for a control ΔnifD strain (DJ2278).
source: We did not detect growth under the same conditions for a control ΔnifD strain (DJ2278, see Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: This is a control experiment result.

claim: The growth observed for ancestral strains did not stem from leaky expression of the alternative, V- or Fe-dependent nitrogen fixation genes in A. vinelandii.
source: This result confirmed that the growth observed for ancestral strains did not stem from leaky expression of the alternative, V- or Fe-dependent nitrogen fixation genes in A. vinelandii, which were left intact.
evidence: This is an inference based on the control experiment result.

claim: A. vinelandii strains harboring only ancestral nifD (Anc1A, Anc2) exhibited mean C2H2 reduction rates of ~5–6 μmol C2H4/mg total protein/hr, ~40–45% that of WT (p ≈ 6e-4 and p ≈ 3e-4, respectively).
source: A. vinelandii strains harboring only ancestral nifD (Anc1A, Anc2) exhibited mean C2H2 reduction rates of ~5–6 μmol C2H4/mg total protein/hr,~40–45% that of WT (p ≈ 6e-4 and p ≈ 3e-4, respectively) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Strain Anc1B, harboring ancestral nifHDK, exhibited a mean acetylene reduction rate of ~9 μmol C2H4/mg total protein/hr, ~70% that of WT (p ≈ 3e-2).
source: Strain Anc1B, harboring ancestral nifHDK, exhibited a mean acetylene reduction rate of ~9 μmol C2H4/mg total protein/hr,~70% that of WT (p ≈ 3e-2).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: The phenotypic variability observed among engineered and WT A. vinelandii strains might result both from differences in nitrogenase expression and nitrogenase activity.
source: The phenotypic variability we observed among engineered and WT A. vinelandii strains might result both from differences in nitrogenase expression and nitrogenase activity.
evidence: This is an inference about the causes of phenotypic variability.

claim: Significant differences in protein quantity relative to WT were not conclusively detected (p>0.05).
source: To provide insights into these disparate effects, we quantified nitrogenase protein expression in engineered strains by immunodetection of ancestral and WT Strep-tagged NifD proteins (the latter from strain DJ2102, see Supplementary file 1c) and did not conclusively detect significant differences in protein quantity relative to WT (p>0.05; Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a finding from protein expression analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Ancestral nitrogenase NifDK protein components were expressed and purified for biochemical characterization.
source: Ancestral nitrogenase NifDK protein components were expressed and purified for biochemical characterization.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.

claim: All ancestral NifDK proteins were assayed with WT NifH protein for reduction of H+, N2, and C2H2.
source: All ancestral NifDK proteins were assayed with WT NifH protein (ancestral NifH proteins were not purified) for reduction of H+, N2, and C2H2.
